newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Milpo seeks new reserves at mine.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Milpo seeks new reserves at mine.

text.p: Minera Milpo SA a polymetallic miner and leading stock on the Lima bolsa, plans to invest $35 million searching for new reserves in its main mine in the Andean highlands, a company official said.
"We are concentrating our efforts in making the central mine deeper to prepare for exploitation in the next few years," the miner's commercial manager, Ernesto Baertl, told Reuters in an interview.

The company has 5.5 million tonnes of proven and probable mineral reserves at its 10 year-old "Milpo" mine in the department of Pasco, 195 miles (315 km) northeast of Lima. It plans to extend its operations by 2,700 feet (800 metres) to a depth of 4,170 feet, he said.
This expansion will probably allow Milpo, whose principal production is zinc and lead, to exploit up to 20 million tonnes of mineral resources, mining analysts said.
Milpo also plans to boost the electricity generating capacity at the mine to 2.5 megawats (MW) at its La Candelaria utility from the current 1.9 MW, Baertl said.
The mine, which needs more than triple its current generating capacity, covers its energy deficit with supply from state-run Electroperu.

Supplementing its search for further reserves at Milpo, the company was working with the United States' Phelps Dodge Corp, hoping to turn its Chacchi copper deposit and polymetallic Cerro Lindo resource into mines, Baertl said.

Despite market confidence that these projects would become full mines, the company official cautioned that up to two more years of studies were needed to ensure that going ahead to the development stage would be profitable.
"They are both still just projects and we still do not have confirmation of their feasibility. But we expect good things since the studies show interesting mineral structures," Baertl said.

If Milpo were to go ahead with these projects, there would be no need for front-end investment for energy supply as the deposits lay close to the country's electricity grid, Baertl said. Cerro Lindo was near the Electro Centro grid, while Chacchi was close to Peru's second city Arequipa, 645 miles (1,030 km) south of Lima, where "there would be no problem" with supply, he added.
The company may have other deposits it could explore but is in no hurry to invest heavily on them until it is clear what the two key deposits can yield.
"We have set out our priorities. We do not want to distract ourselves with adventures," Baertl said.

While Milpo waits for its deposits to come on line, Baerlt is optimistic for the company's balance sheet, believing high international prices are set to continue at least until the first quarter next year.
"We expect zinc to keep these levels in 1997 and for some of 1998 and this represents a shot in the arm for any zinc producing company," Baertl said.

Despite the higher metal prices, Milpo's official projections for improved sales revenue this year appear modest, with a rise to 159 million soles ($60 million), compared to last year's 146 million soles. In the first quarter this year, sales reached 37.6 million soles, compared to 24.8 million in the same period last year.

Investors have been betting on the metal prices translating more obviously into profits and have heavily bought Milpo's stock this year on the Lima Stock Exchange to make it a key player in the mining sector's bull run.
Monday, the miner jumped 10.02 percent to 35.81 soles on volume of 77,000 shares, extending a steady rise which has seen its liquid labor share gain 177.1 percent gain this year.
